name: Gulab Jamun
description: Soft Pakistani gulab jamun made from a tender milk-powder dough, fried slowly for even cooking and soaked in warm cardamom syrup.
ingredients: ¼ cup milk, approximately and added gradually
Neutral oil or ghee for frying
method: Combine the sugar, water and cardamom in a saucepan. Simmer until the sugar is fully dissolved and a light syrup forms; add the optional lemon juice, then keep the syrup warm without boiling it hard.
Mix the milk powder, flour and baking powder evenly. Rub in the ghee, then add milk little by little just until a soft cohesive dough forms; excessive kneading can make the finished jamun dense.
Rest the dough briefly, then divide and roll into small smooth balls. Seal visible cracks before frying because rough or cracked surfaces are more likely to split.

Heat the frying oil or ghee over low to medium-low heat. Add a test ball first if needed, then fry in manageable batches, moving the balls gently so they colour evenly and cook through before becoming too dark.
Let the fried balls rest very briefly, then transfer them to warm—not vigorously boiling—syrup so they can absorb it without a severe temperature shock.
Leave the gulab jamun in the syrup until noticeably softer and well soaked before serving. Keep them in enough syrup that exposed surfaces do not dry out.
tips: Add milk a teaspoon or small splash at a time and stop as soon as the dough holds together; milk powders vary in how much liquid they absorb.
Roll gently between your palms and smooth every visible crack. If the dough starts cracking, lightly moisten your fingers instead of adding lots of extra milk at once.
Fry one test ball first. If it darkens quickly, lower the heat; if it barely colours and absorbs too much oil, allow the oil to warm slightly before continuing.
Keep the balls moving gently in the oil for even colour, but avoid crowding the pan because a large batch can lower the oil temperature.
Keep the syrup warm and pourable, not rapidly boiling or candy-thick. Let the fried balls enter gently and give them time to absorb syrup.
If a ball is browned outside but still dense inside, reduce the frying heat for the next batch and allow more time for the centre to cook before removing it.
storage: Cool leftovers appropriately and refrigerate them covered in their syrup. Warm gently for serving if desired rather than repeatedly heating the whole batch.
image_alt: Soft Pakistani gulab jamun in cardamom sugar syrup with an even deep golden surface
image_caption: Soft gulab jamun fried slowly for an even golden centre-to-edge cook and soaked in warm cardamom syrup.
technique: A tender dough and slow fry matter more than speed. Mix only until the milk-powder dough comes together, smooth surface cracks gently, then fry over controlled low-to-medium heat so the centres cook before the outside becomes dark.
doneness_cues: The dough should feel soft and smooth enough to roll without deep cracks, but not wet or sticky.
Balls should be evenly sized so they cook at the same rate.
Frying should produce gradual, even browning instead of a dark shell within the first minute.
After soaking, gulab jamun should feel soft through the centre and carry syrup inside rather than only on the surface.
mistakes: Kneading aggressively, which can develop a tight dough and dense jamun.
Frying on high heat, creating a dark shell around an undercooked centre.
Rolling cracked balls and expecting syrup to repair the structure.
Dropping very hot fried jamun into aggressively boiling syrup, which can damage texture.
substitutions: Different milk powders absorb moisture differently; add liquid gradually and stop when the dough is workable.
Use a neutral frying oil or a suitable oil-ghee combination according to your preference.
Rose water is optional; cardamom alone can provide a clean syrup aroma.
reheating: Serve at room temperature or warm gently with a little syrup. Avoid boiling soaked gulab jamun because the soft structure can break.

faqs.question: Why are gulab jamun hard inside?
faqs.answer: The dough may be too dry or overworked, or the oil may have been too hot. A slow even fry gives the centre time to cook.

faqs.question: Why do gulab jamun break while frying?
faqs.answer: The dough may be too wet or weak, the balls may have cracks, or the oil temperature may be unstable. Test one ball before frying the batch.

faqs.question: Why are they not absorbing syrup?
faqs.answer: A hard fried shell or syrup that is too concentrated can slow absorption. Fry gradually and keep the syrup pourable rather than candy-thick.

serving: Serve gulab jamun warm or at room temperature with a little of its cardamom syrup spooned over each portion. Garnish lightly with chopped pistachios or almonds if desired; avoid draining the syrup completely, as it keeps the centres moist.
